title: Limits and Derivatives
description: Build intuition for approaching values and interpreting derivatives as rates of change.

lessons.title: Introduction to Limits
objectives: Understand a limit as an approaching value
Evaluate simple limits from tables and expressions

pedagogy.title: Approach, do not plug too fast
pedagogy.content: For limits, first ask what values x approaches and what f(x) approaches, not only f(a).

pedagogy.title: Use nearby values
pedagogy.content: If direct substitution is unclear, test x-values just below and above the target.

content.content: A limit describes the value a function gets close to as x gets close to a number.
As x approaches 3, the values of x+4 approach 7, so the limit is 7.

exercises.question: Compute \lim_{x \to 4}(2x-1).
hints: This is a polynomial expression, so direct substitution works.

exercises.question: Explain in your own words what \lim_{x \to 5} f(x)=2 means.
hints: Use the phrase 'x gets close to 5'.
Describe what f(x) values do near x=5.
exercises.solution: Self-check: as x gets close to 5 (from either side), f(x) gets close to 2.

lessons.title: Derivative as Rate of Change
objectives: Estimate rate of change from simple expressions

pedagogy.title: Derivative means how fast
pedagogy.content: If position changes with time, the derivative tells how fast position changes now.

pedagogy.title: Average vs instantaneous
pedagogy.content: Average rate uses two points. Derivative is the instantaneous rate at one point.

content.content: The derivative f'(x) gives the instantaneous rate of change of f with respect to x.
If f(x)=x^2, then f'(x)=2x. At x=3, the rate is 6.

exercises.question: Given f(x)=x^2 and f'(x)=2x, what is f'(5)?
Sketch y=x^2 and draw a tangent line near x=2. Describe whether slope is positive or negative.
hints: At x=2, the tangent should rise from left to right.
exercises.solution: Self-check: tangent near x=2 should have positive slope (about 4).
